query.original_query: language models generics default reasoning defeasible generalization exceptions birds fly internal representation

sub_queries.semantic_query: internal representation of generics and default reasoning in language models, defeasible generalization handling exceptions like birds fly, circuit mechanisms for typicality and exception suppression
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate how language models represent and reason with generic knowledge and its exceptions, focusing on the internal circuit mechanisms that mediate defeasible generalizations such as "birds fly" while accommodating counterexamples like penguins. Using causal tracing and activation patching on transformer models, we analyze the processing of typicality judgments and exception suppression. Our analysis reveals that factual recall of generic properties is localized to specific MLP layers in the residual stream, while exception handling involves distinct attention heads that modulate feature activation in response to context. We find that the suppression of default inferences for atypical instances relies on a circuit where early-layer attention heads detect exceptional features, and later MLP layers adjust the output distribution to override the generic prediction. Results show that this mechanism is separable from the representation of the generic rule itself, with the exception circuit acting as a corrective override rather than a revision of the stored knowledge. Our findings suggest that default reasoning in language models emerges from the interaction between stable factual representations and context-sensitive suppression circuits.

sub_queries.semantic_query: human cognitive representation of generics and default reasoning, defeasible generalizations exception handling typicality effects birds fly category-based induction
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigated how human reasoners represent and process defeasible generic statements (e.g., “birds fly”) and handle exceptions during category-based induction. Participants completed a speeded truth-value judgment task and a property inference task using stimuli that varied in typicality (e.g., robins vs. penguins for “birds fly”). We measured response times and endorsement rates for generic statements paired with typical and atypical exemplars. Results indicate that typicality strongly modulates both the speed and likelihood of endorsing a generic, with atypical exemplars eliciting significantly longer latencies and lower endorsement rates, consistent with the hypothesis that generics are represented as default generalizations with exception-handling mechanisms. Furthermore, in the inference task, participants generalized novel properties from typical to atypical category members less readily when the property was framed as a generic rule, suggesting that default reasoning relies on a similarity-based typicality gradient rather than strict logical quantification. Findings support the view that human generic cognition employs probabilistic, prototype-based representations that allow flexible exception handling without abandoning the generalization.

papers.title: Grokked Transformers are Implicit Reasoners: A Mechanistic Journey to the Edge of Generalization
papers.research_question: Can transformers learn implicit reasoning over parametric knowledge, and how does grokking enable this? What are the differences in systematic generalization between composition and comparison tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers can learn implicit reasoning over parametric knowledge through grokking, but systematic generalization varies: composition fails out-of-distribution while comparison succeeds. Mechanistic analysis reveals the formation of generalizing circuits and explains the differences, guiding data and training setups and suggesting architectural improvements.
papers.conclusion: Transformers are capable of learning implicit reasoning through grokking, but the level of systematic generalization depends on the task and the circuit configuration. The findings guide data and training setups and suggest improvements to the transformer architecture for better cross-layer memory sharing.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers can learn implicit reasoning only through grokking (extended training far beyond overfitting).
The speed of grokking correlates with the ratio of inferred to atomic facts (data distribution), not the absolute training data size.
For composition, transformers fail to generalize systematically to out-of-distribution examples, while for comparison, they succeed.
Mechanistic analysis reveals distinct generalizing circuits: for composition, a sequential circuit that stores atomic facts in separate layers; for comparison, a parallel circuit that stores atomic facts in the same layer.
In a complex reasoning task with a large search space, a fully grokked transformer achieves near-perfect accuracy, while state-of-the-art LLMs with non-parametric memory (GPT-4-Turbo, Gemini-1.5-Pro) fail regardless of prompting or retrieval augmentation.
papers.limitation:
The task formulation (induction and application of inference rules from atomic and inferred facts) may not apply to the full spectrum of reasoning types.
The study is limited to synthetic tasks and may not fully capture real-world reasoning complexities.
future_direction: Developing cross-layer memory-sharing mechanisms for transformers (e.g., memory-augmentation, explicit recurrence) to improve systematic generalization.
Investigating the tradeoff between parametric and non-parametric memory in language models.
Understanding the role of verbalizations (e.g., chain-of-thought) in teaching models to reason implicitly.
papers.abstract: We study whether transformers can learn to implicitly reason over parametric knowledge, a skill that even the most capable language models struggle with. Focusing on two representative reasoning types, composition and comparison, we consistently find that transformers can learn implicit reasoning, but only through grokking, i.e., extended training far beyond overfitting. The levels of generalization also vary across reasoning types: when faced with out-of-distribution examples, transformers fail to systematically generalize for composition but succeed for comparison. We delve into the model's internals throughout training, conducting analytical experiments that reveal: 1) the mechanism behind grokking, such as the formation of the generalizing circuit and its relation to the relative efficiency of generalizing and memorizing circuits, and 2) the connection between systematicity and the configuration of the generalizing circuit. Our findings guide data and training setup to better induce implicit reasoning and suggest potential improvements to the transformer architecture, such as encouraging cross-layer knowledge sharing. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for a challenging reasoning task with a large search space, GPT-4-Turbo and Gemini-1.5-Pro based on non-parametric memory fail badly regardless of prompting styles or retrieval augmentation, while a fully grokked transformer can achieve near-perfect accuracy, showcasing the power of parametric memory for complex reasoning.

papers.title: Circuit Stability Characterizes Language Model Generalization
papers.research_question: Can circuit stability characterize and predict generalization in language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces circuit stability as a method to assess model performance and shows it can characterize and predict different aspects of generalization.
papers.conclusion: Circuit stability characterizes generalization in language models and provides an actionable way to assess and improve model performance.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit stability predicts length, structural, and compositional generalization in arithmetic reasoning tasks.
Circuit instability in arithmetic indicates lack of understanding of commutativity and associativity.
For Boolean expression evaluation, circuit non-equivalence indicates structural generalization issues.
Chain-of-thought prompting induces circuit stability and improves performance.
Circuit stability is a robust estimator of model performance that can be computed efficiently.
papers.limitation:
Empirical case studies are limited in terms of tasks and models.
Computational cost of circuit discovery can be high for very large models.
Constructing partitions manually requires prior knowledge of the task.
future_direction: Extending circuit stability to other modalities and architectures.
Investigating the connection between circuit stability and generalization bounds.
Automating the construction of partitions for complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Extensively evaluating the capabilities of (large) language models is difficult. Rapid development of state-of-the-art models induce benchmark saturation, while creating more challenging datasets is labor-intensive. Inspired by the recent developments in mechanistic interpretability, we introduce circuit stability as a new way to assess model performance. Circuit stability refers to a model's ability to apply a consistent reasoning process-its circuit-across various inputs. We mathematically formalize circuit stability and circuit equivalence. Then, through three case studies, we empirically show that circuit stability and the lack thereof can characterize and predict different aspects of generalization. Our proposed methods offer a step towards rigorously relating the generality of models to their interpretability.

papers.title: Reasoning Circuits in Language Models: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Syllogistic Inference
papers.research_question: How is content-independent syllogistic reasoning internalized in LMs during pre-training? Are content-independent mechanisms disentangled from world knowledge and belief biases? Does the core reasoning mechanism generalize across syllogistic schemes, model sizes, and architectures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a sufficient and necessary circuit for syllogistic reasoning involving middle-term suppression, showing that LMs learn transferable content-independent reasoning mechanisms that are susceptible to contamination from world knowledge.
papers.conclusion: LMs learn transferable reasoning mechanisms but such mechanisms are contaminated and suppressed by the world knowledge acquired during pre-training, indicating a lack of generalizable abstract logical primitives.
papers.key_findings:
The circuit for syllogistic reasoning involves a three-stage mechanism: long induction, duplication, suppression, and mover heads.
The circuit is necessary and sufficient for symbolic syllogistic reasoning.
The circuit transfers to non-symbolic arguments but is contaminated by belief biases, with additional attention heads encoding world knowledge.
The circuit generalizes across unconditionally valid syllogistic schemes where models achieve high accuracy.
The suppression mechanism pattern is compatible across different model families and sizes, though with increasing complexity in larger models.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is confined to specific syllogistic reasoning templates and does not consider more complex scenarios.
The experimentation is confined due to the intricate level of granularity and computational complexity required in circuit analysis.
future_direction: Further studies to understand how the discovered symbolic circuit can be effectively disentangled from world knowledge to enable systematic generalization in LMs’ reasoning.
papers.abstract: Recent studies on reasoning in language models (LMs) have sparked a debate on whether they can learn systematic inferential principles or merely exploit superficial patterns in the training data. To understand and uncover the mechanisms adopted for formal reasoning in LMs, this paper presents a mechanistic interpretation of syllogistic inference. Specifically, we present a methodology for circuit discovery aimed at interpreting content-independent and formal reasoning mechanisms. Through two distinct intervention methods, we uncover a sufficient and necessary circuit involving middle-term suppression that elucidates how LMs transfer information to derive valid conclusions from premises. Furthermore, we investigate how belief biases manifest in syllogistic inference, finding evidence of partial contamination from additional attention heads responsible for encoding commonsense and contextualized knowledge. Finally, we explore the generalization of the discovered mechanisms across various syllogistic schemes, model sizes and architectures. The identified circuit is sufficient and necessary for syllogistic schemes on which the models achieve high accuracy (>60%), with compatible activation patterns across models of different families. Overall, our findings suggest that LMs learn transferable content-independent reasoning mechanisms, but that, at the same time, such mechanisms do not involve generalizable and abstract logical primitives, being susceptible to contamination by the same world knowledge acquired during pre-training.

papers.title: Toward Mechanistic Explanation of Deductive Reasoning in Language Models
papers.research_question: How does a small language model solve a deductive reasoning task, and what internal mechanisms (e.g., induction heads) are involved in implementing the logical inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a small language model can learn deductive reasoning by implementing rule-based circuits, with induction heads playing a central role, and introduces a truncated pseudoinverse technique for decoding query, key, and value information.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that a tiny LM can learn deductive reasoning by implementing symbolic rule-based circuits, with induction heads being a fundamental component, and suggests that induction heads may also be central in more complex logical reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
A simplified NanoGPT model trained with Chain-of-Thought can learn deductive reasoning rules and generalize to unseen examples.
Induction heads are crucial for implementing rule completion and rule chaining steps in the logical inference.
The model learns the underlying inference rules rather than memorizing patterns.
A single attention head can host multiple induction heads and other circuits, simplifying post-hoc explanation.
Training without Chain-of-Thought leads to memorization and poor generalization, indicating the importance of CoT for learning rules.
papers.limitation:
The interpretability techniques used (e.g., residual stream decoding and truncated pseudoinverse) are not 100% precise and may fail to decode the expected tokens.
The deductive reasoning task is simple and does not reflect the complexity of real-world logical reasoning.
future_direction: Investigating whether one-layer circuits resembling induction heads can be created by modifying the attention mechanism to decouple key and value positions.
Exploring the role of induction heads in solving more complex logical problems with larger language models.
papers.abstract: Recent large language models have demonstrated relevant capabilities in solving problems that require logical reasoning; however, the corresponding internal mechanisms remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we show that a small language model can solve a deductive reasoning task by learning the underlying rules (rather than operating as a statistical learner). A low-level explanation of its internal representations and computational circuits is then provided. Our findings reveal that induction heads play a central role in the implementation of the rule completion and rule chaining steps involved in the logical inference required by the task.

papers.title: Reasoning as State Transition: A Representational Analysis of Reasoning Evolution in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How does reasoning ability evolve during training in large language models, and what is the role of internal representation dynamics in this process?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a representational analysis framework showing that post-training yields limited improvement in static initial representation quality, but reasoning involves a continuous distributional shift in representations during generation, which post-training enhances to drive representations toward a better state for task solving.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a novel representational perspective on reasoning evolution in LLMs, highlighting the importance of internal state dynamics and the role of post-training in enhancing state transitions, offering insights for future model analysis and optimization.
papers.key_findings:
Post-training yields only limited improvement in static initial representation quality.
Reasoning involves a significant continuous distributional shift in representations during generation, unlike non-reasoning tasks.
Post-training empowers models to drive this representation transition toward a better distribution for task solving.
There is a high correlation between generation correctness and final representations, but low correlation with initial representations.
The semantic content of the generated tokens is the dominant driver of the state transition, not additional computation or intrinsic parameter differences.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models have achieved remarkable performance on reasoning tasks, motivating research into how this ability evolves during training. Prior work has primarily analyzed this evolution via explicit generation outcomes, treating the reasoning process as a black box and obscuring internal changes. To address this opacity, we introduce a representational perspective to investigate the dynamics of the model's internal states. Through comprehensive experiments across models at various training stages, we discover that post-training yields only limited improvement in static initial representation quality. Furthermore, we reveal that, distinct from non-reasoning tasks, reasoning involves a significant continuous distributional shift in representations during generation. Comparative analysis indicates that post-training empowers models to drive this transition toward a better distribution for task solving. To clarify the relationship between internal states and external outputs, statistical analysis confirms a high correlation between generation correctness and the final representations; while counterfactual experiments identify the semantics of the generated tokens, rather than additional computation during inference or intrinsic parameter differences, as the dominant driver of the transition. Collectively, we offer a novel understanding of the reasoning process and the effect of training on reasoning enhancement, providing valuable insights for future model analysis and optimization.

papers.title: Calibrating Reasoning in Language Models with Internal Consistency
papers.research_question: How can internal representations in large language models be used to calibrate reasoning, specifically by measuring inconsistencies between intermediate and final layers during chain-of-thought reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes internal consistency as a novel measure to evaluate LLM confidence in reasoning by examining agreement of latent predictions from intermediate layers, and shows that up-weighting paths with high internal consistency significantly boosts reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: Internal consistency is a robust indicator of correct reasoning paths and can be leveraged to enhance the reliability of reasoning in LLMs through calibration.
papers.key_findings:
CoT reasoning leads to inconsistencies between middle and final layer representations, indicating uncertainty.
Internal consistency effectively distinguishes between correct and incorrect reasoning paths.
Up-weighting reasoning paths with high internal consistency improves reasoning accuracy across various tasks.
Patterns in attention and feed-forward networks across layers provide insights into the emergence of internal inconsistency.
Layer-weighted aggregation of internal consistency finds transferable patterns that generalize across tasks.
papers.limitation:
The study is restricted to decoder-only models.
The analysis focuses on vanilla chain-of-thought prompting, not other complex prompting techniques.
future_direction: Extending the concept of internal consistency to encoder-decoder models.
Investigating internal consistency under more complex prompting scenarios.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in various reasoning tasks, aided by techniques like chain-of-thought prompting that elicits verbalized reasoning. However, LLMs often generate text with obvious mistakes and contradictions, raising doubts about their ability to robustly process and utilize generated rationales. In this work, we investigate reasoning in LLMs through the lens of internal representations, focusing on how these representations are influenced by generated rationales. Our preliminary analysis reveals that while generated rationales improve answer accuracy, inconsistencies emerge between the model's internal representations in middle layers and those in final layers, potentially undermining the reliability of their reasoning processes. To address this, we propose internal consistency as a measure of the model's confidence by examining the agreement of latent predictions decoded from intermediate layers. Extensive empirical studies across different models and datasets demonstrate that internal consistency effectively distinguishes between correct and incorrect reasoning paths. Motivated by this, we propose a new approach to calibrate reasoning by up-weighting reasoning paths with high internal consistency, resulting in a significant boost in reasoning performance. Further analysis uncovers distinct patterns in attention and feed-forward modules across layers, providing insights into the emergence of internal inconsistency. In summary, our results demonstrate the potential of using internal representations for self-evaluation of LLMs. Our code is available at github.com/zhxieml/internal-consistency.

papers.title: Emergent Symbolic Mechanisms Support Abstract Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What internal mechanisms support abstract reasoning in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies an emergent three-stage symbolic architecture in LLMs that implements abstract reasoning via symbol abstraction heads, symbolic induction heads, and retrieval heads.
papers.conclusion: LLMs perform abstract reasoning via emergent symbolic mechanisms, suggesting a resolution to the debate between symbolic and neural network approaches.
papers.key_findings:
Symbol abstraction heads in early layers convert input tokens to abstract variables based on relations.
Symbolic induction heads in intermediate layers perform sequence induction over abstract variables.
Retrieval heads in later layers retrieve the token associated with the predicted abstract variable.
These mechanisms are robust across multiple abstract reasoning tasks and model families.
Representations in these heads encode abstract variables invariant to specific tokens, and better representation correlates with correct performance.
papers.abstract: Many recent studies have found evidence for emergent reasoning capabilities in large language models (LLMs), but debate persists concerning the robustness of these capabilities, and the extent to which they depend on structured reasoning mechanisms. To shed light on these issues, we study the internal mechanisms that support abstract reasoning in LLMs. We identify an emergent symbolic architecture that implements abstract reasoning via a series of three computations. In early layers, symbol abstraction heads convert input tokens to abstract variables based on the relations between those tokens. In intermediate layers, symbolic induction heads perform sequence induction over these abstract variables. Finally, in later layers, retrieval heads predict the next token by retrieving the value associated with the predicted abstract variable. These results point toward a resolution of the longstanding debate between symbolic and neural network approaches, suggesting that emergent reasoning in neural networks depends on the emergence of symbolic mechanisms.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Propositional Logical Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally perform propositional logical reasoning? What computational strategies do they employ?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a coherent computational architecture for propositional logical reasoning in Qwen3 models, comprising four interlocking mechanisms: Staged Computation, Information Transmission, Fact Retrospection, and Specialized Attention Heads.
papers.conclusion: The investigation uncovers a coherent computational architecture for propositional logical reasoning, with four interlocking mechanisms that generalize across model scales, rule types, and reasoning depths, suggesting fundamental computational strategies rather than task-specific shortcuts.
papers.key_findings:
The model organizes reasoning into staged computation: early layers process facts, middle layers process logical expressions, and late layers aggregate for prediction.
Information transmission occurs through segment-terminal tokens (boundary tokens) that act as information hubs.
Fact retrospection: the model persistently re-accesses source fact tokens throughout the network depth.
Specialized attention heads: splitting heads (early layers), transmission heads (middle layers), and fact-retrieval heads (middle to late layers) implement the above mechanisms.
These mechanisms generalize across model scales (8B and 14B), rule types (11 categories), and reasoning depths (one-hop and two-hop).
papers.limitation:
The internal computations within MLP layers remain largely unexplored.
The analysis does not explain how or when these mechanisms emerge during training.
Cannot definitively rule out that these patterns reflect sophisticated statistical shortcuts rather than genuine logical algorithms.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to deeper reasoning chains (i.e., three-hop and beyond).
Investigating diverse model architectures beyond the Qwen family (e.g., Llama, Mistral, etc.).
Analyzing training dynamics to reveal how and when these mechanisms emerge during pretraining.
papers.abstract: Understanding how Large Language Models (LLMs) perform logical reasoning internally remains a fundamental challenge. While prior mechanistic studies focus on identifying taskspecific circuits, they leave open the question of what computational strategies LLMs employ for propositional reasoning. We address this gap through comprehensive analysis of Qwen3 (8B and 14B) on PropLogic-MI, a controlled dataset spanning 11 propositional logic rule categories across one-hop and two-hop reasoning. Rather than asking ''which components are necessary,'' we ask ''how does the model organize computation?'' Our analysis reveals a coherent computational architecture comprising four interlocking mechanisms: Staged Computation (layer-wise processing phases), Information Transmission (information flow aggregation at boundary tokens), Fact Retrospection (persistent re-access of source facts), and Specialized Attention Heads (functionally distinct head types). These mechanisms generalize across model scales, rule types, and reasoning depths, providing mechanistic evidence that LLMs employ structured computational strategies for logical reasoning.

papers.title: Reason to Rote: Rethinking Memorization in Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do language models memorize label noise, and why does such memorization not heavily affect generalizable reasoning capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Memorization of noisy labels in language models builds on, rather than overrides, the underlying reasoning mechanisms, with memories stored via distributed encoding and outlier heuristics in neurons.
papers.conclusion: The findings show that memorization of label noise builds on existing reasoning mechanisms, using distributed encoding and outlier heuristics, explaining the phenomenon of benign memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Models first learn to generalize on noisy training instances (predicting correct labels) before memorizing the noisy labels.
Even when producing memorized noisy labels, models continue to compute intermediate reasoning outputs corresponding to the correct labels.
Memorization and generalization circuits substantially overlap, indicating memorization builds on existing generalization mechanisms.
Memorization uses distributed encoding across multiple input tokens and intermediate results rather than a simple lookup.
In the FDA task, memorization occurs via 'outlier heuristics' where higher-layer MLP neurons slightly shift their activation patterns to fit noisy labels.
papers.limitation:
Focus on relatively small language models; larger models might exhibit different behaviors.
Models trained from scratch, so influence of pretraining data is not considered.
Examination of implicit reasoning without explicit solution steps; not studying models with explicit chain-of-thought.
future_direction: Study memorization in larger models
Investigate effect of pretraining on memorization and reasoning
Study memorization in models with explicit chain-of-thought reasoning
papers.abstract: Large language models readily memorize arbitrary training instances, such as label noise, yet they perform strikingly well on reasoning tasks. In this work, we investigate how language models memorize label noise, and why such memorization in many cases does not heavily affect generalizable reasoning capabilities. Using two controllable synthetic reasoning datasets with noisy labels, four-digit addition (FDA) and two-hop relational reasoning (THR), we discover a reliance of memorization on generalizable reasoning mechanisms: models continue to compute intermediate reasoning outputs even when retrieving memorized noisy labels, and intervening reasoning adversely affects memorization. We further show that memorization operates through distributed encoding, i.e., aggregating various inputs and intermediate results, rather than building a look-up mechanism from inputs to noisy labels. Moreover, our FDA case study reveals memorization occurs via outlier heuristics, where existing neuron activation patterns are slightly shifted to fit noisy labels. Together, our findings suggest that memorization of label noise in language models builds on, rather than overrides, the underlying reasoning mechanisms, shedding lights on the intriguing phenomenon of benign memorization.

papers.title: Arithmetic Without Algorithms: Language Models Solve Math With a Bag of Heuristics
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) solve arithmetic reasoning tasks by learning robust generalizable algorithms or by memorizing training data?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs solve arithmetic tasks by combining a sparse set of heuristic neurons, each implementing simple patterns, forming a 'bag of heuristics' rather than using a robust algorithm or memorization.
papers.conclusion: LLMs implement a bag of heuristics—a combination of many memorized rules—to perform arithmetic reasoning, rather than using robust algorithms or pure memorization.
papers.key_findings:
A sparse subset of MLP neurons in the arithmetic circuit implements simple heuristics for arithmetic.
Each heuristic neuron activates for specific input patterns and promotes corresponding answer tokens.
The combination of these heuristic neurons (a bag of heuristics) explains most of the model's accuracy on arithmetic prompts.
This mechanism emerges early in training and persists as the main source of arithmetic accuracy.
The bag of heuristics fails to generalize perfectly, leading to errors when prompts lack sufficient associated heuristics or when heuristics have imperfect recall.
papers.limitation:
Human bias in defining heuristic types, as abstractions are based on human-identifiable definitions.
Analysis focuses on LLMs that tokenize multi-digit numbers as single tokens, which may not generalize to models with single-digit tokenization.
future_direction: Developing methods to identify heuristic abstractions without human bias.
Investigating if regularization can improve the bag of heuristics mechanism.
Exploring fundamental changes to training and architectures to improve mathematical abilities.
papers.abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) solve reasoning tasks by learning robust generalizable algorithms, or do they memorize training data? To investigate this question, we use arithmetic reasoning as a representative task. Using causal analysis, we identify a subset of the model (a circuit) that explains most of the model's behavior for basic arithmetic logic and examine its functionality. By zooming in on the level of individual circuit neurons, we discover a sparse set of important neurons that implement simple heuristics. Each heuristic identifies a numerical input pattern and outputs corresponding answers. We hypothesize that the combination of these heuristic neurons is the mechanism used to produce correct arithmetic answers. To test this, we categorize each neuron into several heuristic types-such as neurons that activate when an operand falls within a certain range-and find that the unordered combination of these heuristic types is the mechanism that explains most of the model's accuracy on arithmetic prompts. Finally, we demonstrate that this mechanism appears as the main source of arithmetic accuracy early in training. Overall, our experimental results across several LLMs show that LLMs perform arithmetic using neither robust algorithms nor memorization; rather, they rely on a "bag of heuristics".

papers.title: Are formal and functional linguistic mechanisms dissociated in language models?
papers.research_question: Do current large language models exhibit distinct localization (dissociation) of formal and functional linguistic mechanisms in their internal circuits?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds evidence for formal-functional dissociation in LLMs in terms of cross-task faithfulness (formal task circuits perform other formal tasks better than functional ones, and vice-versa), but not in terms of circuit overlap, suggesting a shared pool of mechanisms for formal tasks rather than a single unified region.
papers.conclusion: There is evidence for emerging formal-functional dissociation in LLMs in terms of cross-task faithfulness, but not in terms of circuit overlap, indicating a set of shared formal linguistic mechanisms rather than a single unified region.
papers.key_findings:
Circuits for formal and functional linguistic tasks have low overlap (IoU).
Circuits for formal tasks do not have especially high overlap with each other, arguing against a single unified formal network.
Formal task circuits perform other formal tasks better than they perform functional tasks (cross-task faithfulness).
Functional task circuits perform other functional tasks better than they perform formal tasks (cross-task faithfulness).
Clustering based on cross-task faithfulness vectors separates formal and functional tasks into distinct groups.
papers.limitation: The circuit-finding method (EAP-IG) may not perfectly capture all relevant mechanisms, and the findings are limited to the specific models and tasks studied.
future_direction: Studying more models and tasks to generalize findings.
Using more granular analyses (e.g., neuron-level, sparse feature circuits).
Investigating the effects of model scale and architecture on dissociation.
papers.abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) are increasingly capable, these capabilities are unevenly distributed: they excel at formal linguistic tasks, such as producing fluent, grammatical text, but struggle more with functional linguistic tasks like reasoning and consistent fact retrieval. Inspired by neuroscience, recent work suggests that to succeed on both formal and functional linguistic tasks, LLMs should use different mechanisms for each; such localization could either be built-in or emerge spontaneously through training. In this paper, we ask: do current models, with fast-improving functional linguistic abilities, exhibit distinct localization of formal and functional linguistic mechanisms? We answer this by finding and comparing the "circuits", or minimal computational subgraphs, responsible for various formal and functional tasks. Comparing 5 LLMs across 10 distinct tasks, we find that while there is indeed little overlap between circuits for formal and functional tasks, there is also little overlap between formal linguistic tasks, as exists in the human brain. Thus, a single formal linguistic network, unified and distinct from functional task circuits, remains elusive. However, in terms of cross-task faithfulness - the ability of one circuit to solve another's task - we observe a separation between formal and functional mechanisms, suggesting that shared mechanisms between formal tasks may exist.

papers.title: Opening the Black Box: A Survey on the Mechanisms of Multi-Step Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms that enable multi-step reasoning in large language models, covering both implicit (latent) and explicit (e.g., Chain-of-Thought) reasoning paradigms?
papers.core_contribution: This survey provides a comprehensive overview of the mechanisms underlying multi-step reasoning in large language models, organizing existing research around seven interconnected research questions and highlighting future research directions.
papers.conclusion: The survey concludes by highlighting five open research directions for future mechanistic understanding of multi-step reasoning in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Implicit multi-hop reasoning in LLMs is an orchestrated, layered process with distinct modules specializing in different phases, but it is constrained by the fixed depth of transformers.
Implicit reasoning capability emerges via grokking, a phase transition from memorization to generalization, influenced by training data distribution, data scale, and optimization biases.
LLMs frequently bypass genuine multi-step reasoning by using shortcuts, such as direct input-output associations (factual shortcuts) or surface-level heuristics (structural shortcuts).
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting activates a 'reasoning mode' where models use generated tokens as external memory, breaking the depth limitation and enhancing computational expressiveness and generalization.
CoT does not equate to faithful explainability; it often functions as post-hoc rationalization due to a structural mismatch between the distributed, parallel computation of transformers and the sequential nature of explicit reasoning.
future_direction: Rigorous causal analysis in real-world settings
Bridging the faithfulness gap of explicit CoT reasoning
Mechanistic understanding of Latent CoT reasoning
White-box evaluation metrics for LLM reasoning
From mechanistic interpretation to model control
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable abilities to solve problems requiring multiple reasoning steps, yet the internal mechanisms enabling such capabilities remain elusive. Unlike existing surveys that primarily focus on engineering methods to enhance performance, this survey provides a comprehensive overview of the mechanisms underlying LLM multi-step reasoning. We organize the survey around a conceptual framework comprising seven interconnected research questions, from how LLMs execute implicit multi-hop reasoning within hidden activations to how verbalized explicit reasoning remodels the internal computation. Finally, we highlight five research directions for future mechanistic studies.

papers.title: Analysing Neural Language Models: Contextual Decomposition Reveals\n Default Reasoning in Number and Gender Assignment
papers.research_question: How do neural language models (specifically LSTMs) process grammatical phenomena such as number agreement and gender anaphora resolution? What information do they base their decisions on, and do they exhibit default reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Generalised Contextual Decomposition (GCD), a method to decompose LSTM predictions into contributions from input phrases and model biases, and uses it to reveal that LSTM language models employ default reasoning for number and gender assignment, with singular and masculine as defaults encoded in the model weights.
papers.conclusion: GCD is a powerful method for analyzing LSTM language models, revealing default reasoning in number and gender assignment, and can be extended to other models and improved with better Shapley value approximations.
papers.key_findings:
LSTM language models exhibit a default reasoning effect: singular and masculine are default categories hard-coded in the model weights.
For number agreement, plural verb predictions depend strongly on the subject, while singular verb predictions rely more on other sentence elements and model intercepts.
For gender anaphora, the model has a male default bias; predicting female pronouns requires explicit evidence from female referents.
The model shows gender bias in stereotypical gender roles: male-stereotyped job titles lead to male pronoun preference, but female-stereotyped job titles do not lead to a female preference.
GCD enables detailed analysis of anaphora resolution in language models, pinpointing where and how resolution takes place.
future_direction: Extending GCD to attention-based models
Improving the gate factorisation with better Shapley value approximators
Exploring the axiomatic approach to relate GCD to other explanation methods
papers.abstract:
Extensive research has recently shown that recurrent neural language models
are able to process a wide range of grammatical phenomena. How these models are
able to perform these remarkable feats so well, however, is still an open
question. To gain more insight into what information LSTMs base their decisions
on, we propose a generalisation of Contextual Decomposition (GCD). In
particular, this setup enables us to accurately distil which part of a
prediction stems from semantic heuristics, which part truly emanates from
syntactic cues and which part arise from the model biases themselves instead.
We investigate this technique on tasks pertaining to syntactic agreement and
co-reference resolution and discover that the model strongly relies on a
default reasoning effect to perform these tasks.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Large Reasoning Models: A Survey of Training, Inference, and Failures
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms that drive the reasoning behaviors and failures of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs)?
papers.core_contribution: This survey synthesizes recent research on the mechanistic understanding of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), organizing insights into training dynamics, reasoning mechanisms, and unintended behaviors to bridge the gap between performance and transparency.
papers.conclusion: The survey highlights the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework to advance the mechanistic understanding of LRMs.
papers.key_findings:
SFT expands exploratory paths while RL compresses them, leading to entropy reduction and performance gains.
RL training follows a two-stage process where basic skills are acquired first, followed by the emergence of reasoning abilities.
LRMs exhibit unique reasoning structures, including cyclical processes and topological properties, driven by key behavioral primitives.
Hallucinations in LRMs are influenced by RL, which reduces abstention and can increase incorrect answers.
Chain-of-thought reasoning in LRMs is often unfaithful, with a disconnect between internal states and verbalized traces.
papers.limitation:
The rapid development of LRM research means that new findings may not be captured in this survey.
The survey focuses primarily on language models, excluding multimodal capabilities.
The discussion is limited to traditional LLM architectures, excluding newer approaches like diffusion-based LLMs.
future_direction: Applied interpretability for training-time and inference-time improvements
Development of scalable and generalizable mechanistic interpretability frameworks
Establishment of a unified theoretical framework for reasoning in LRMs
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has catalyzed the emergence of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) that have pushed reasoning capabilities to new heights. While their performance has garnered significant excitement, exploring the internal mechanisms driving these behaviors has become an equally critical research frontier. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of the mechanistic understanding of LRMs, organizing recent findings into three core dimensions: 1) training dynamics, 2) reasoning mechanisms, and 3) unintended behaviors. By synthesizing these insights, we aim to bridge the gap between black-box performance and mechanistic transparency. Finally, we discuss under-explored challenges to outline a roadmap for future mechanistic studies, including the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework.

papers.title: Benchmarking and Understanding Compositional Relational Reasoning of LLMs
papers.research_question: What is the capability of existing transformer large language models (LLMs) in solving compositional relational reasoning (CRR) tasks, and what are the underlying mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the Generalized Associative Recall (GAR) benchmark for evaluating compositional relational reasoning in LLMs, revealing their deficiency, and discovers core circuits and True/False attention heads that are fundamental for CRR.
papers.conclusion: The GAR benchmark is challenging for mainstream LLMs and reveals a fundamental deficiency in compositional relational reasoning. Mechanistic interpretability analysis discovers reusable core circuits and identifies True/False attention heads that play fundamental roles in CRR across models and tasks.
papers.key_findings:
GAR is challenging for existing LLMs, with performance dropping significantly for harder tasks and the compositionality gap increasing with model scale.
Attribution patching reveals core circuits reused by Vicuna-33B across different GAR tasks, including a truthfulness sub-circuit and an in-context learning sub-circuit.
Intervention experiments show that correct functioning of identified vital attention heads (e.g., predicting, pre-predicting, higher-order local, induction, and relating heads) significantly impacts task performance.
Two classes of higher-order relating heads (True and False heads) are identified whose activations represent the abstract notion of true and false in GAR tasks.
The activation patterns of the True/False heads generalize to other datasets (SNLI and GoT), indicating they encode information for truthfulness classification beyond GAR.
papers.limitation: The circuit discovery is done manually without using automatic circuit discovery methods, which is left for future work.
future_direction: Automatic circuit discovery methods for larger models and more complex circuits.
papers.abstract: Compositional relational reasoning (CRR) is a hallmark of human intelligence, but we lack a clear understanding of whether and how existing transformer large language models (LLMs) can solve CRR tasks. To enable systematic exploration of the CRR capability of LLMs, we first propose a new synthetic benchmark called Generalized Associative Recall (GAR) by integrating and generalizing the essence of several tasks in mechanistic interpretability (MI) study in a unified framework. Evaluation shows that GAR is challenging enough for existing LLMs, revealing their fundamental deficiency in CRR. Meanwhile, it is easy enough for systematic MI study. Then, to understand how LLMs solve GAR tasks, we use attribution patching to discover the core circuits reused by Vicuna-33B across different tasks, and a set of vital attention heads. Intervention experiments show that the correct functioning of these heads significantly impacts task performance. Especially, we identify two classes of heads whose activations represent the abstract notion of true and false in GAR tasks respectively. They play fundamental roles in CRR across various models and tasks.

papers.title: A Modular Dataset to Demonstrate LLM Abstraction Capability
papers.research_question: Do LLMs have an internal representation of reasoning correctness and abstraction in reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs internally encode representations of reasoning correctness, with strongest signals in middle-late layers, and they distinguish between logical and semantic equivalence in abstract reasoning concepts.
papers.conclusion: LLMs possess internal representations of reasoning correctness and abstraction, which can inform future efforts to enhance model reliability, interpretability, and trustworthiness.
papers.key_findings:
A classifier trained on LLM activations achieves over 80% accuracy in predicting reasoning step correctness.
LLMs have internal representations of reasoning correctness, strongest in middle-late Transformer layers.
LLMs encode abstract reasoning concepts that separate logical from semantic equivalence.
Abstraction level varies across layers, with middle layers containing more abstract information.
The reasoning representations are similar across top-performing layers, suggesting redundant encoding.
papers.limitation:
Analysis restricted to structured logic puzzles, may not generalize to real-world scenarios.
Classifier's success may not generalize to other types of reasoning problems.
Reliance on probing techniques does not provide mechanistic explanation of how representations emerge.
Classifier trained on single LLM architecture, generalizability across models unclear.
future_direction: Explore more diverse reasoning benchmarks.
Conduct broader cross-model analyses including LRM models.
Develop methods for directly steering LLM reasoning based on learned representations.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit impressive capabilities but struggle with reasoning errors due to hallucinations and flawed logic. To investigate their internal representations of reasoning, we introduce ArrangementPuzzle, a novel puzzle dataset with structured solutions and automated stepwise correctness verification. We trained a classifier model on LLM activations on this dataset and found that it achieved over 80% accuracy in predicting reasoning correctness, implying that LLMs internally distinguish between correct and incorrect reasoning steps, with the strongest representations in middle-late Transformer layers. Further analysis reveals that LLMs encode abstract reasoning concepts within the middle activation layers of the transformer architecture, distinguishing logical from semantic equivalence. These findings provide insights into LLM reasoning mechanisms and contribute to improving AI reliability and interpretability, thereby offering the possibility to manipulate and refine LLM reasoning.

papers.title: Knowledge Circuits in Pretrained Transformers
papers.research_question: How do transformers store and express knowledge through collaborative circuits of components such as attention heads and MLPs, and how can these circuits be used to analyze model behaviors and knowledge editing?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces knowledge circuits as a method to uncover how transformers store and express knowledge through collaborative components, and demonstrates their utility in analyzing knowledge editing and model behaviors like hallucinations and in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: Knowledge circuits provide a valuable framework for understanding how transformers store and express knowledge, and can inform the design of better knowledge editing methods.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge circuits effectively capture knowledge representations, maintaining over 70% of original performance with less than 10% of the graph.
Knowledge is aggregated in early-to-middle layers and enhanced in later layers.
Special components like mover heads and relation heads are critical for information transfer and relational capture.
ROME editing incorporates information at the edited layer, while fine-tuning directly writes knowledge and dominates predictions.
Hallucinations occur when the circuit lacks effective mover heads or they select incorrect information.
papers.limitation:
Coarse granularity of circuits, not capturing fine-grained neuron-level behavior.
Logit lens method may have discrepancies between middle layers and output unembedding matrix.
future_direction: Finer-grained circuit analysis at the neuron level.
Developing more robust techniques to map intermediate representations to outputs (e.g., Attention Lens).
Investigating activation mechanisms of reused heads and polysemanticity.
papers.abstract: The remarkable capabilities of modern large language models are rooted in their vast repositories of knowledge encoded within their parameters, enabling them to perceive the world and engage in reasoning. The inner workings of how these models store knowledge have long been a subject of intense interest and investigation among researchers. To date, most studies have concentrated on isolated components within these models, such as the Multilayer Perceptrons and attention head. In this paper, we delve into the computation graph of the language model to uncover the knowledge circuits that are instrumental in articulating specific knowledge. The experiments, conducted with GPT2 and TinyLLAMA, have allowed us to observe how certain information heads, relation heads, and Multilayer Perceptrons collaboratively encode knowledge within the model. Moreover, we evaluate the impact of current knowledge editing techniques on these knowledge circuits, providing deeper insights into the functioning and constraints of these editing methodologies. Finally, we utilize knowledge circuits to analyze and interpret language model behaviors such as hallucinations and in-context learning. We believe the knowledge circuits hold potential for advancing our understanding of Transformers and guiding the improved design of knowledge editing. Code and data are available in https://github.com/zjunlp/KnowledgeCircuits.

papers.title: Function Induction and Task Generalization: An Interpretability Study with Off-by-One Addition
papers.research_question: What mechanisms inside large language models drive task-level generalization via in-context learning, specifically through the lens of off-by-one addition?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a 'function induction' mechanism in transformer language models that explains how they generalize from seen to unseen tasks via in-context learning, particularly for multi-step tasks like off-by-one addition.
papers.conclusion: The findings offer deeper insights into how reusable and composable structures within language models enable task-level generalization.
papers.key_findings:
The model's generalization from standard addition to off-by-one addition is explained by a circuit resembling induction heads but operating at a function level, termed 'function induction'.
The induction of the +1 function is governed by multiple attention heads (FI heads) in parallel, each emitting a distinct piece of the function.
The same function induction mechanism is reused in a broader range of tasks, including shifted multiple-choice QA, Caesar cipher, and base-8 addition.
The circuit involves three groups of attention heads: consolidation heads (Group 1), function induction heads (Group 2), and previous token heads (Group 3).
The mechanism is found across multiple models (Gemma-2, Mistral, Llama-2, Llama-3), though with variations.
papers.limitation: The exact role of consolidation heads and why they emerge remains limited, relating to the broader challenge of interpreting 'negative' behavior in language models.
future_direction: Finer-grained interpretation of consolidation heads and their role.
Further investigation into the differences between FI heads and FV heads (function vector heads).
Training toy models to perform off-by-one addition and isolating the circuit requires separate study.
papers.abstract: Large language models demonstrate the intriguing ability to perform unseen tasks via in-context learning. However, it remains unclear what mechanisms inside the model drive such task-level generalization. In this work, we approach this question through the lens of off-by-one addition (i.e., 1+1=3, 2+2=5, 3+3=?), a two-step, counterfactual task with an unexpected +1 function as a second step. Leveraging circuit-style interpretability techniques such as path patching, we analyze the models' internal computations behind their performance and present three key findings. First, we uncover a function induction mechanism that explains the model's generalization from standard addition to off-by-one addition. This mechanism resembles the structure of the induction head mechanism found in prior work and elevates it to a higher level of abstraction. Second, we show that the induction of the +1 function is governed by multiple attention heads in parallel, each of which emits a distinct piece of the +1 function. Finally, we find that this function induction mechanism is reused in a broader range of tasks, including synthetic tasks such as shifted multiple-choice QA and algorithmic tasks such as base-8 addition. Overall, our findings offer deeper insights into how reusable and composable structures within language models enable task-level generalization.

papers.title: Exploring the Hidden Reasoning Process of Large Language Models by Misleading Them
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) truly engage in task abstraction and rule-based reasoning beyond mere memorization?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Misleading Fine-Tuning (MisFT), an evaluation paradigm free from data contamination, and finds that LLMs can generalize contradictory rules to novel domains, suggesting an internal abstraction-reasoning mechanism.
papers.conclusion: MisFT provides evidence that LLMs possess human-like reasoning abilities through abstraction and rule-based reasoning, and it can serve as a tool for assessing generalization in various tasks and modalities.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can learn contradictory arithmetic rules through fine-tuning and apply them to solve math word problems, showing out-of-distribution generalization.
Larger models exhibit better generalization performance, indicating a positive correlation between model size and reasoning ability.
LLMs can generalize overloaded logical rules from formulas to natural language reasoning tasks in first-order logic.
Vision-language models (VLMs) can generalize contradictory rules learned from text to image-based arithmetic problems without seeing images during fine-tuning.
Deep layers in LLMs are crucial for abstraction and reasoning, as freezing them sharply reduces generalization accuracy on math word problems.
papers.limitation:
The paper does not pinpoint the actual circuits for abstraction and reasoning in the model's computational graph, leaving it for future work.
MisFT may cause catastrophic forgetting and is a disruptive probing method that could harm the model's general reasoning ability.
future_direction: Accurately pinpointing the circuits for abstraction and reasoning using more advanced mechanistic interpretation methods.
Applying MisFT to assess reasoning and generalization capabilities in a wider range of tasks and modalities.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been able to perform various forms of reasoning tasks in a wide range of scenarios, but are they truly engaging in task abstraction and rule-based reasoning beyond mere memorization? To answer this question, we propose a novel experimental approach, Misleading Fine-Tuning (MisFT), to examine whether LLMs perform abstract reasoning by altering their original understanding of fundamental rules. In particular, by constructing datasets with math expressions or logical formulas that contradict correct principles, we fine-tune the model to learn those contradictory rules and assess its generalization ability on unseen test domains. Through a series of experiments, we find that current LLMs are capable of applying contradictory rules to solve practical math word problems and natural language reasoning tasks, implying the presence of an internal mechanism in LLMs that abstracts before reasoning.

papers.title: A Implies B: Circuit Analysis in LLMs for Propositional Logical Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do large language models solve propositional logic problems? Are their reasoning mechanisms localized and modular, and what are the core components involved?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that LLMs use sparse, modular circuits for propositional logical reasoning, consisting of four families of attention heads with specialized roles: queried-rule locating, queried-rule moving, fact processing, and decision making. These circuits are similar across different models but show scale-dependent variations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs employ sparse, modular circuits for propositional logical reasoning, with specialized attention head families. These circuits are similar across models but exhibit scale-dependent differences, suggesting that mechanistic insights do not fully generalize across model sizes.
papers.key_findings:
All three models contain four families of attention heads with specialized roles: queried-rule locating heads, queried-rule mover heads, fact-processing heads, and decision heads.
The models perform lazy reasoning: the core circuit activates primarily after seeing the Question and the query variable.
The models reuse sub-circuits for different parts of the argument when possible.
Gemma-2-27B has additional logical-operator heads and a more parallel circuit compared to the more sequential Gemma-2-9B.
Small trained models (3-layer) perform intermingled reasoning, less modular than larger pre-trained models.
papers.limitation: Partial analysis of Gemma-2-27B due to computational constraints
future_direction: Fully validating the algorithm for LogOp chain reasoning in small transformers
papers.abstract: Due to the size and complexity of modern large language models (LLMs), it has proven challenging to uncover the underlying mechanisms that models use to solve reasoning problems. For instance, is their reasoning for a specific problem localized to certain parts of the network? Do they break down the reasoning problem into modular components that are then executed as sequential steps as we go deeper in the model? To better understand the reasoning capability of LLMs, we study a minimal propositional logic problem that requires combining multiple facts to arrive at a solution. By studying this problem on Mistral and Gemma models, up to 27B parameters, we illuminate the core components the models use to solve such logic problems. From a mechanistic interpretability point of view, we use causal mediation analysis to uncover the pathways and components of the LLMs' reasoning processes. Then, we offer fine-grained insights into the functions of attention heads in different layers. We not only find a sparse circuit that computes the answer, but we decompose it into sub-circuits that have four distinct and modular uses. Finally, we reveal that three distinct models -- Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B and Gemma-2-27B -- contain analogous but not identical mechanisms.

papers.title: Is Grokking Worthwhile? Functional Analysis and Transferability of Generalization Circuits in Transformers
papers.research_question: Is a grokked model superior to its non-grokked counterparts on downstream tasks? Furthermore, is the extensive computational cost of waiting for the grokking phase worthwhile?
papers.core_contribution: Grokking does not represent genuine acquisition of generalized reasoning; instead, it integrates memorized facts into naturally established circuits, and grokked transformers show limited transferability to novel facts.
papers.conclusion: Grokking merely integrates memorized facts into naturally established circuits, and grokked transformers have limited transferability to novel facts, suggesting a trade-off between data scarcity and computational resources.
papers.key_findings:
Non-grokked and grokked models follow identical reasoning paths on in-distribution compositional queries, indicating that grokking is the process of integrating memorized atomic facts into an established reasoning structure.
Grokking and the formation of a Generalization Circuit are not intrinsically linked; behavioral grokking can occur without circuit formation.
Generalization Circuits exhibit limited transferability; they do not imply full mastery of compositional logic and struggle with new facts in certain positions.
papers.limitation:
Computational constraints limit exhaustive exploration of fake grokking due to prolonged training cycles.
Findings are constrained to parameter-sharing Transformer architectures and may not extend to standard transformers.
future_direction: Systematically categorize which data distributions favor circuit formation over pattern memorization.
papers.abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at factual retrieval, they often struggle with the "curse of two-hop reasoning" in compositional tasks. Recent research suggests that parameter-sharing transformers can bridge this gap by forming a "Generalization Circuit" during a prolonged "grokking" phase. A fundamental question arises: Is a grokked model superior to its non-grokked counterparts on downstream tasks? Furthermore, is the extensive computational cost of waiting for the grokking phase worthwhile? In this work, we conduct a mechanistic study to evaluate the Generalization Circuit's role in knowledge assimilation and transfer. We demonstrate that: (i) The inference paths established by non-grokked and grokked models for in-distribution compositional queries are identical. This suggests that the "Generalization Circuit" does not represent the sudden acquisition of a new reasoning paradigm. Instead, we argue that grokking is the process of integrating memorized atomic facts into an naturally established reasoning path. (ii) Achieving high accuracy on unseen cases after prolonged training and the formation of a certain reasoning path are not bound; they can occur independently under specific data regimes. (iii) Even a mature circuit exhibits limited transferability when integrating new knowledge, suggesting that "grokked" Transformers do not achieve a full mastery of compositional logic.

papers.title: Analysing Neural Language Models: Contextual Decomposition Reveals Default Reasoning in Number and Gender Assignment
papers.research_question: How do LSTM language models process syntactic agreement and co-reference resolution, and what information do they rely on for these tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Generalised Contextual Decomposition (GCD), a method to analyze LSTM language models, and reveals that the models rely on a default reasoning effect (singular and masculine as defaults) for number agreement and gender pronoun resolution.
papers.conclusion: GCD is a powerful method for analyzing LSTM language models, revealing a default reasoning effect in number and gender assignment. The method can be extended to other models and improved with better Shapley value approximations.
papers.key_findings:
The model uses a default reasoning effect: singular and masculine are default categories encoded in the model weights.
For number agreement, plural verbs depend strongly on the subject, while singular verbs do not.
For gender pronoun resolution, the model has a male bias encoded in the intercepts, and female pronouns require explicit evidence.
The model correctly resolves referents for unambiguous gender but shows stereotypical biases for gender-neutral job titles.
GCD can accurately attribute contributions of input phrases and model intercepts to predictions.
future_direction: Extending GCD to attention-based models
Improving gate factorisation with better Shapley value approximators
papers.abstract: Extensive research has recently shown that recurrent neural language models are able to process a wide range of grammatical phenomena. How these models are able to perform these remarkable feats so well, however, is still an open question. To gain more insight into what information LSTMs base their decisions on, we propose a generalisation of Contextual Decomposition (GCD). In particular, this setup enables us to accurately distil which part of a prediction stems from semantic heuristics, which part truly emanates from syntactic cues and which part arise from the model biases themselves instead. We investigate this technique on tasks pertaining to syntactic agreement and co-reference resolution and discover that the model strongly relies on a default reasoning effect to perform these tasks.

papers.title: Disentangling Recall and Reasoning in Transformer Models through Layer-wise Attention and Activation Analysis
papers.research_question: Does recall and reasoning in transformer models rely on overlapping or separable internal circuits?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that recall and reasoning in transformer models rely on partially distinct internal circuits, with early layers supporting recall and deeper layers enabling reasoning, supported by causal evidence from interventions.
papers.conclusion: The Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct model develops a hierarchically organized division between recall and reasoning, with early layers for recall and deeper layers for reasoning, supported by task-specific attention heads and MLP neurons.
papers.key_findings:
Layer specialization: early layers (0–6) predominantly support factual recall, while later layers (17–27) concentrate on reasoning.
Head-level differentiation: 74% of attention heads show significant task preferences, with recall-preferring heads in shallower layers and reasoning-preferring heads in deeper layers.
MLP neuron selectivity: roughly one-third of MLP neurons exhibit task-specific activation patterns, with clusters in layers 4 (recall) and 22 (reasoning).
Selective impairment: disabling recall-associated circuits reduces factual accuracy by up to 15% while leaving reasoning unaffected, and vice versa for reasoning circuits.
Consistency: these specialization patterns are statistically stable across cross-validation and robust to normalization choices.
future_direction: Extend experiments to larger, contemporary models such as LLaMA and Mistral.
Expand the dataset to encompass more diverse reasoning phenomena.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models excel at both recall (retrieving memorized facts) and reasoning (performing multi-step inference), but whether these abilities rely on distinct internal mechanisms remains unclear. Distinguishing recall from reasoning is crucial for predicting model generalization, designing targeted evaluations, and building safer interventions that affect one ability without disrupting the other.We approach this question through mechanistic interpretability, using controlled datasets of synthetic linguistic puzzles to probe transformer models at the layer, head, and neuron level. Our pipeline combines activation patching and structured ablations to causally measure component contributions to each task type. Across two model families (Qwen and LLaMA), we find that interventions on distinct layers and attention heads lead to selective impairments: disabling identified "recall circuits" reduces fact-retrieval accuracy by up to 15\% while leaving reasoning intact, whereas disabling "reasoning circuits" reduces multi-step inference by a comparable margin. At the neuron level, we observe task-specific firing patterns, though these effects are less robust, consistent with neuronal polysemanticity.Our results provide the first causal evidence that recall and reasoning rely on separable but interacting circuits in transformer models. These findings advance mechanistic interpretability by linking circuit-level structure to functional specialization and demonstrate how controlled datasets and causal interventions can yield mechanistic insights into model cognition, informing safer deployment of large language models.

papers.title: Circuit Component Reuse Across Tasks in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether circuit components are reused across different tasks in transformer language models, and whether insights from circuit analysis generalize across tasks.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that circuit components are reused across different tasks in transformer language models, and that interventions based on one circuit can improve performance on another task, providing evidence for task-general algorithmic building blocks.
papers.conclusion: Circuit components are reused across tasks, providing evidence that large language models' behavior can be explained in terms of a relatively small number of interpretable task-general algorithmic building blocks.
papers.key_findings:
The IOI circuit reproduces on GPT2-Medium, with minor differences such as the negative mover head attending only to the S2 token.
The Colored Objects circuit shares about 78% of the important attention heads with the IOI circuit, indicating high component reuse.
Interventions on inhibition heads and the negative mover head can boost accuracy on the Colored Objects task from 49.6% to 93.7%.
The inhibition-mover head subcircuit behaves invariantly across tasks, as predicted by the IOI circuit.
The negative mover head in GPT2-Medium exhibits more sophisticated behavior than in GPT2-Small, directly demoting the subject token.
papers.limitation:
Quantifying circuit overlap is complex and not fully addressed in this paper.
The generality of the circuit beyond the studied tasks is not confirmed.
future_direction: Understanding how commonly the mover circuit is used by GPT2 in other tasks.
Developing methods for quantifying circuit overlap.
Studying circuit reuse in larger models.
papers.abstract: Recent work in mechanistic interpretability has shown that behaviors in language models can be successfully reverse-engineered through circuit analysis. A common criticism, however, is that each circuit is task-specific, and thus such analysis cannot contribute to understanding the models at a higher level. In this work, we present evidence that insights (both low-level findings about specific heads and higher-level findings about general algorithms) can indeed generalize across tasks. Specifically, we study the circuit discovered in Wang et al. (2022) for the Indirect Object Identification (IOI) task and 1.) show that it reproduces on a larger GPT2 model, and 2.) that it is mostly reused to solve a seemingly different task: Colored Objects (Ippolito & Callison-Burch, 2023). We provide evidence that the process underlying both tasks is functionally very similar, and contains about a 78% overlap in in-circuit attention heads. We further present a proof-of-concept intervention experiment, in which we adjust four attention heads in middle layers in order to 'repair' the Colored Objects circuit and make it behave like the IOI circuit. In doing so, we boost accuracy from 49.6% to 93.7% on the Colored Objects task and explain most sources of error. The intervention affects downstream attention heads in specific ways predicted by their interactions in the IOI circuit, indicating that this subcircuit behavior is invariant to the different task inputs. Overall, our results provide evidence that it may yet be possible to explain large language models' behavior in terms of a relatively small number of interpretable task-general algorithmic building blocks and computational components.

papers.title: Emergence of symbolic abstraction heads for in-context learning in large language models
papers.research_question: How do small transformer models recognize, learn, and generalize abstract sequential symbolic patterns, and do they form internal symbolic representations through abstraction heads?
papers.core_contribution: Small transformer models can learn abstract symbolic patterns and develop abstraction heads for in-context learning, enabling symbolic reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Small transformer models can recognize and generalize abstract patterns through abstraction heads, providing insights for neuro-symbolic processing.
papers.key_findings:
Models with 2 or 3 layers successfully solve abstract pattern matching tasks, while 1-layer models fail.
Abstraction heads emerge in attention mechanisms, attending to the first instantiation to generalize patterns.
Variable matching is a simpler task that can be solved even by single-layer models without abstraction.
Training loss shows bumps that correlate with sudden improvements in accuracy, indicating learning of critical strategies.
Abstraction heads operate at a more abstract level than induction heads, focusing on pattern matching from instantiations.
papers.limitation:
The experiments are based on simplified sequences of numbers and may not generalize to human language or complex relations.
The study is limited to small transformer models with 1-3 layers, and different mechanisms may emerge in larger models.
future_direction: Investigate alternative mechanisms for abstract pattern matching in transformers.
Explore the emergence of abstraction heads in larger models with more layers.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) based on self-attention circuits are able to perform, at inference time, novel reasoning tasks, but the mechanisms inside the models are currently not fully understood. We assume that LLMs are able to generalize abstract patterns from the input and form an internal symbolic internal representation of the content. In this paper, we study this by analyzing the performance of small LLM models trained with sequences of instantiations of abstract sequential symbolic patterns or templates. It is shown that even a model with two layers is able to learn an abstract template and use it to generate correct output representing the pattern. This can be seen as a form of symbolic inference taking place inside the network. In this paper, we call the emergent mechanism abstraction head. Identifying mechanisms of symbolic reasoning in a neural network can help to find new ways to merge symbolic and neural processing.

papers.title: It is not True that Transformers are Inductive Learners: Probing NLI Models with External Negation
papers.research_question: Do transformer models fine-tuned on NLI tasks learn to reason logically, specifically with respect to external negation and the law of excluded middle?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer models fine-tuned on NLI tasks fail to inductively learn the law of excluded middle for external negation, indicating they do not learn logical reasoning but instead rely on shallow heuristics.
